title: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)
hook: the Gita is over, Arjuna has picked up his bow, and Yudhishthira takes off his armor and walks toward the enemy.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Bhishma Parva, Arjuna saw the universal form, heard Bhishma's name among the fallen, and asked for his friend's familiar face, saying at last, now I'm myself again. Whose face did you come back to? Day eight hundred twenty-four.

The teaching ends. Arjuna tells Krishna his confusion is gone and he will do as Krishna says. He picks up his bow. Both armies roar. And then, before a single arrow flies, Yudhishthira does something strange. He takes off his armor. He lays down his weapons. And he climbs out of his chariot and walks, on foot, straight toward the enemy lines. His brothers run after him, asking where he's going. The other army starts to murmur that he's come to surrender. Session six of six: what the Gita leads into.
screen: `ARJUNA PICKS UP HIS BOW` → `YUDHISHTHIRA TAKES OFF HIS ARMOR` → `WALKING TOWARD THE ENEMY`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira walks to Bhishma, bows to him, and asks his permission to fight him, and his blessing. Read that right after the Gita. Krishna has just taught that a warrior must do his duty. Here is a man about to do exactly that: fight his grandfather, and honor him first. Bhishma is moved. In Ganguli's telling, he says that if Yudhishthira had not come to him like this, he would have cursed him with defeat. Instead he blesses him. Fight, he says, and win. Then he says something painfully honest about himself. A person is a slave to wealth, but wealth is no one's slave. I am bound to the Kauravas by their wealth. Ask me for anything except to fight on your side. So Yudhishthira asks a harder question. How can you be beaten in battle? And Bhishma tells him: no one can defeat me now, and the time of my death has not yet come. Ask me again another time. Yudhishthira goes on to his teachers, Drona and Kripa, and to his uncle Shalya, and does the same with each. Then, standing between the armies, he calls out: anyone who chooses us, we'll choose them. And one of Dhritarashtra's own sons, Yuyutsu, crosses the field to the Pandava side. That's how the Gita sits in its place. It ends, and the very next thing is a man walking unarmed into the enemy's ranks, to honor the people he must fight.
screen: `HE BOWS AND ASKS A BLESSING` · `BHISHMA: I'M BOUND BY THEIR WEALTH` · `HOW CAN YOU BE BEATEN? ASK AGAIN` · then, large: `YUYUTSU CROSSES OVER`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath slow. Think of someone you're at odds with, a little or a lot. You don't have to fix anything. Just picture yourself setting down whatever you carry against them for one minute, the way Yudhishthira set down his armor. Breathing in, see their face. Breathing out, find one thing in them you can honestly respect. Stay with that one thing. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Bhishma Parva. The book of the grandsire who blesses his opponent, confesses what binds him, and says: ask me again.
Your line: ask me again another time. Today, before a disagreement, say one honest word of respect to the other person first. Day eight hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: In the Mahabharata, the Gita is followed directly by Yudhishthira's unarmed walk to Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Shalya to ask their blessing.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli (Bhishma Parva, the section after the Gita): Yudhishthira doffs his armor and walks toward the Kauravas; brothers and Krishna follow; Kaurava soldiers think he comes in fear; Bhishma says he would have cursed him had he not come; 'man is the slave of wealth, but wealth is no one's slave'; bound by the Kauravas' wealth; asks what he wants except fighting for him; on how he can be vanquished, says no one can defeat him now and his time of death has not come, and to come again.
Yuyutsu's crossing follows Yudhishthira's call to anyone who would choose the Pandavas; confirm wording.
The script does not quote Drona's or Shalya's replies.
Editor pass: cut 'without hatred' from the summary of the Gita's teaching, which the cited verses do not frame that way.

Audit (fresh pass): checked against the scene after the Gita; no changes needed. Its practice/carry theme (respect before disagreement) is close to day 814's fair-peace carry; a Keeper may want a different angle.
